food.text: West African cooking is changing. In the past West Africans ate much less meat and used native oils, palm oil on the coast and shea butter in Sahelian regions, but today the diet is much heavier in meats, salt, and fats.

Huge swaths of West African forest are being razed to clear space for palm oil and cocoa plantations, and even acacias are hacked away for cooking fires to feed growing families. In 2005, the Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations ranked Nigeria as the state with the worst deforestation rate in the world.

Recent famines in Africa include the 2005-06 Niger food crisis and the 2010 Sahel famine. In 2012, a month-long heatwave and drought put over ten million people in the western Sahel at risk of famine, according to the Methodist Relief and Development Fund.

Jollof rice, also called benachin, is a popular dish all over West Africa. It originated in Senegal and has since spread across the region, especially to Nigeria and Ghana, and its name comes from the Wolof ethnic group.

Corn has gained significant ground across West Africa because it is cheap, swells to greater volumes and makes a white final product that is greatly desired. Banku and kenkey are both maize dough staples, with kenkey originating in Ghana.
Yam is mainly produced in West Africa. Côte d'Ivoire, Ghana, Togo, Benin, Nigeria and Cameroon together account for 97% of African yam production.

Dambou is a couscous-like dish from Niger, often made with rice, millet or other grain and traditionally including moringa leaves. In France it has been adapted as couscous aux épinards, a variant of Maghreb-style couscous that often uses spinach in place of the moringa.

In the Sahel, couscous made from millet or sorghum is a very popular traditional staple. It is frequently prepared with okra or baobab leaves mixed in to improve digestibility and texture, and it can be mixed with yogurt to make Chakery, a dessert or snack.
Malt drinks such as Supermalt and fresh coconut water are popular beverages in West Africa. Drinks made from roselle, like Zobo, are popular too, and so is tea.

Palm wine, a common West African alcoholic drink, is made from the fermented sap of various palm trees. It is usually sold sweet, when less fermented and retaining more of the sap's sugar, or sour, when fermented longer and stronger. Beer from millet is also common.
Fura is a common drink, especially across northern Nigeria. It is made of cooked, then pounded, millet or sorghum with a little cow's milk.

art.text: The Great Mosque of Djenné had been established in the 14th century but was demolished in the early 19th century. It was rebuilt in 1906 to 1907 under Ismaila Traoré, with guidance from French engineers. Today it is the largest earthen building in sub-Saharan Africa.

Calls for the return of the Benin Bronzes began within the palace itself. Oba Eweka II raised the matter in the 1910s, and Oba Akenzua II renewed it in the 1930s, focusing on royal regalia such as ceremonial stools.
art.source_title: Art of the Kingdom of Benin

art.text: The Museum of West African Art in Benin City, Nigeria, was designed by architect David Adjaye, who revealed renderings in November 2020. It was planned to open on 11 November 2025, but on 9 November, during preview events, followers of Oba Ewuare II attacked the private preview ceremony and the previews were curtailed. The museum remains closed until further notice. It is meant to focus mainly on contemporary West African art.

Under French colonial rule in the Sahel, French engineers and architects helped popularize a "Neo-Sudanese" style. It was based on local traditional architecture but emphasized symmetry and monumentality.
Djenné, famous for its distinctive adobe architecture, was designated a World Heritage Site by UNESCO in 1988. The historic centre of Agadez in Niger was inscribed on the World Heritage List in 2013.

The first formal request from the Nigerian state for Benin Bronzes came in 1972, when Ekpo Eyo, Director of the Federal Department of Antiquities, wrote to European museums. European institutions largely ignored it. Eyo later helped draft the 1970 UNESCO Convention on the Illicit Transfer of Cultural Property and the 1972 World Heritage Convention.
art.source_title: Art of the Kingdom of Benin

art.text: In April 2021, Germany agreed to return to present-day Nigeria the Benin bronzes its troops had looted from the Kingdom of Benin. In late 2021 the Smithsonian Museum of African Art removed its Benin bronzes from display, saying it planned to repatriate them.
art.source_title: Art of the Kingdom of Benin

art.text: The terracotta sculptures of the Nok culture were first discovered in 1928 at the village of Nok in southern Kaduna State, Nigeria, which gave the culture its name. Some sculptures show hunters with slingshots, bows and arrows, and one shows two people paddling a dugout canoe with their goods.
The rebuilt Great Mosque of Djenné served as a model for other mosques in the region. One example is the Grand Mosque of Mopti, built by the French administration in 1935.
Djenné's adobe buildings need replastering at least every other year, and the Great Mosque is replastered every year. Even so, in 2009 one of its minarets collapsed after heavy rainfall.

In 1973, General Yakubu Gowon, then head of state, walked into the Nigerian National Museum in Lagos and took one of the Benin heads. He gifted it to Queen Elizabeth, and it remains in Britain's Royal Collection. Critics cite the incident when they fear mismanagement of returned art.
art.source_title: Art of the Kingdom of Benin

art.text: A 1984 survey of Djenné identified 134 two-storey buildings of significant architectural importance. By 1995, despite World Heritage restrictions, 30% of those buildings had been demolished, most replaced with new adobe buildings. Between 1996 and 2003 the Dutch government funded a project to restore around 100 older buildings.

In 2021, eight small mosques in northern Côte d'Ivoire were inscribed on the World Heritage list. They exemplify a special type of Volta Basin religious architecture, and were probably originally built between the 17th and 19th centuries.
In 1980, the West African CFA franc's 10 and 25 franc coins were redesigned. One depicted a family using a water pump, and the other a young woman with chemistry tools.

war.text: In 2012, AQIM and its Islamist allies captured the northern half of Mali. They held the territory for almost a year, until a French-led foreign intervention forced them out of the urban areas. That intervention was succeeded by the Sahel-wide Operation Barkhane.

In September 1940 the Allies tried to capture the port of Dakar in French West Africa, in an operation called Operation Menace. They hoped to replace the pro-German Vichy administration with a Free French one under General Charles de Gaulle. The fighting included shore batteries duelling with the Allied fleet, air raids and dogfights in which several British Swordfish were shot down, and 4 of the 9 Swordfish aircrew on the attack on the Richelieu were killed. The Vichy submarines Persée and Ajax were sunk, the destroyer L'Audacieux was set on fire and beached, and the Allies withdrew, leaving Dakar in Vichy hands.

French West Africa saw little major fighting in World War II. Only one large-scale action took place there, the Battle of Dakar from 23 to 25 September 1940. The region stayed under Vichy France's control until the Allied invasion of North Africa in November 1942.
war.source_title: French West Africa in World War II

war.text: Since Mali's independence, there have been four rebellions involving Tuareg people: from 1962 to 1964, from 1990 to 1995, from 2007 to 2009, and again since 2012. In 1990, opposition movements began to emerge amid a turbulent rise of ethnic violence in the north, after many Tuaregs who had migrated to Algeria and Libya during the drought returned. In the rebellion that began in 2012, the conflict in the north increased cases of kidnapping and rape. Ex-slaves were a vulnerable population, with reports of some being recaptured by their former masters, and Islamist groups that had helped the Tuareg defeat the government turned on them.

Before attacking Dakar, the Allies tried to persuade the Vichy French defenders to let them enter peacefully. They first used propaganda, then tried to take the city by force of arms. Both attempts ended in defeat, and Free French efforts shifted to French Equatorial Africa.
war.source_title: French West Africa in World War II

war.text: Unlike in metropolitan France, the French Colonial Troops in West Africa were not reduced after the 1940 armistice. The Axis powers also interfered little in the region. This made the troops a valuable addition to the forces of Free France once the region was liberated.
war.source_title: French West Africa in World War II

war.text: Starting in 2008, al-Qaeda in the Islamic Maghreb began kidnapping groups of tourists in the Sahel. In January 2009, four tourists were kidnapped near the Mali–Niger border after attending a cultural festival at Anderamboukané, and one of them was subsequently murdered. In November 2011, gunmen attacked tourists at a hotel in Timbuktu, killing one and kidnapping three others. Visitors to Timbuktu fell from around 6000 in 2009 to only 492 in the first four months of 2011.

During the Battle of Dakar, the French battleship Richelieu was hit by two 15-inch shells from the British battleship Barham. Over two days Richelieu's 380mm main guns fired a total of 24 rounds. Guns 7 and 8 in her turret number 2 failed on the first round, and her reconditioned propellant charges reduced range and caused fire-control problems. One of her 380mm rounds fell short of Barham, and the blast forced the ship's side inwards for 7 feet, causing minor flooding.

Tension between the French and neighbouring British colonies, particularly Sierra Leone, led to the formation of the Freetown Defence Flight in June 1941. No military incidents took place. Anti-British sentiment had run high since the French battleship Richelieu was hit at Dakar on 10 July 1940.
war.source_title: French West Africa in World War II

literature.text: Some Timbuktu manuscripts are written in African languages, including Fula, Songhay, Tamasheq, Bambara and Soninke, using the Arabic script. This writing practice is known as Ajami. The collection's dates run into the early 20th century, until the decline of traditional education in French Sudan.

Between 2012 and 2013, 4,203 of Timbuktu's manuscripts were burned or stolen after the fall of the city in the Northern Mali conflict. The Islamist rebels of Ansar Dine were responsible. The manuscripts had been preserved for centuries in the homes of local families.

In a 2021 analysis of the SAVAMA-DCI libraries, the largest collection of historical documents from Timbuktu, Charles C. Stewart found that most were not ancient. They were mostly 20th century writings, along with copies of Islamic works from the Middle East and North Africa. Stewart says they open a window on the intellectual makeup of Islamic Africa in the twentieth century.

About 90% of the manuscripts at risk during the 2012 to 2013 conflict were saved by the population, organized around the NGO SAVAMA-DCI. Some 350,000 manuscripts were transported to safety. In 2022, 300,000 of them were still in Bamako.

Among the 20,000 SAVAMA-DCI records containing author information, Charles C. Stewart found only four texts from Timbuktu's Golden Age in the 16th century. Three were only one page long, and the fourth was eleven pages long. He noted that the hype about the manuscripts embodying classical Islamic learning is not reflected in the libraries' contents.

The Ahmed Baba Institute and a library, both holding thousands of manuscripts, were said to have been burnt as the Islamists retreated from Timbuktu. The fires came after Ansar Dine's takeover of the city during the Northern Mali conflict.

In 1970, UNESCO founded an organization whose tasks included preserving the Timbuktu manuscripts, but it went unfunded until 1977. Real funding arrived after 1998, when Harvard professor Henry Louis Gates visited Timbuktu for his PBS series Wonders of the African World. The series raised public and academic awareness of the manuscripts.

The Ghanaian politician Kwame Nkrumah popularised the phrase University of Sankore in 1961. Yet there is no evidence that Timbuktu had an organised educational institution equivalent to a medieval or modern university. The label endures as shorthand for the scholarship of the city's community of scholars and students.

In 2009, the cultural TV channel ARTE produced a feature-length film on Timbuktu's manuscript heritage, called Tombouctou: les manuscrits sauvés des sables. Another 2009 film, Manuscripts of Timbuktu, was made by South African director Zola Maseko.

science.text: From the mid 20th century, as more archaeological data became available, scholars began to favor a purely local origin for the Ghana Empire. Their work combined archaeology, geographical sources written between 830 and 1400 CE, the Tarikhs from the 16th and 17th centuries, and oral traditions.

Households in Timbuktu, Mali, preserved a huge number of manuscripts for centuries, including works on art, medicine, philosophy and science. Research and digitisation efforts on them began only in the 20th and 21st centuries.

In 1969 Patrick Munson excavated at Dhar Tichitt, a site associated with the ancestors of the Soninke. It revealed a complex culture present by 1600 BCE, with architectural and material elements similar to those found at Koumbi Saleh in the 1920s.

In 2006 the Talo Dam was built on the Bani River to irrigate parts of the floodplain near San. It retains 0.18 km3 of water, which is 1.3% of the river's average annual discharge of 13.4 km3 for 1952 to 2002.
Mali was ranked 135th out of 139 in the Global Innovation Index in 2025. Its economy centres on agriculture and mining, with gold representing 80% of its exports.

In his 2021 analysis of the SAVAMA-DCI libraries, Charles C. Stewart found that most Timbuktu documents were of 20th century origin, not medieval. Of 20,000 records with author information, only four dated from the 16th century. He said they offer a unique opening to the intellectual makeup of Islamic Africa in the twentieth century.

French archaeologists began excavating Koumbi Saleh in the 1920s. Paul Thomassey and Raymond Mauny dug there in 1949 to 1950, and another French team worked from 1975 to 1981. Even so, the royal town with its large palace and burial mounds has not been located.

The Talo Dam is 43 km west of San and 110 km upstream from Djenné. The African Development Bank's environmental impact assessment was criticised for not fully considering downstream hydrology, and the dam is expected to delay the annual flood's arrival and reduce its intensity.

The Timbuktu Manuscripts Project, run by the University of Cape Town, was founded in 2003 and is the first official cultural project of the New Partnership for Africa's Development. It released a report in 2008, and its online database is accessible to researchers only. In 2015 it was announced the Timbuktu trust fund would close.

politics.text: After World War II, nationalist movements arose across West Africa. In 1957 Ghana, under Kwame Nkrumah, became the first West African colony to achieve independence. By 1974, the region's nations were entirely autonomous.

French West Africa was a federation of eight colonial territories: Mauritania, Senegal, French Sudan, French Guinea, Ivory Coast, Upper Volta, Dahomey and Niger. With an area of 4,689,000 square kilometres, it was eight times the size of Metropolitan France.

When the Gold Coast became independent in 1957 under Kwame Nkrumah, it named itself Ghana. The name recalls the ancient Ghana Empire, which was based in what is now southeast Mauritania and western Mali.

Mali replaced French with 13 African languages as its official languages in 2022, after French had been the official language until then. Bambara is the first language of the majority of Mali's population.

Nigeria has Africa's largest Muslim population. In 1999 its northern states adopted the Sharia penal code, though punishments have been rare. Dozens of women sentenced to stoning to death for adultery were later freed.

Mali became independent in 1960, after a brief federation with Senegal, and was then established as the Republic of Mali. Under one-party rule, political opponents were arrested, and Fily Dabo Sissoko died in prison in Kidal, supposedly on Keïta's orders, though this is not confirmed. In January 1991, peaceful student protests were brutally suppressed, with mass arrests and torture of leaders and participants. In March 1991, soldiers opened fire indiscriminately on nonviolent demonstrators, an estimated 300 people died over four days, and dozens more were massacred on 26 March under Traoré's orders. A coup then brought down Traoré and led to a new constitution and a democratic, multi-party state.

Vichy France kept control of French West Africa after the fall of France in June 1940. Its only large-scale action was the Battle of Dakar, 23 to 25 September 1940, when Allied forces failed to persuade the Vichy defenders to let them enter peacefully. Both a propaganda attempt and an attack by force ended in defeat.
politics.source_title: French West Africa in World War II

politics.text: The Loi Cadre of 23 June 1956 brought universal suffrage to elections in all French African colonies. The first such elections in French West Africa were the municipal elections of late 1956. Territorial Assembly elections followed in each of the eight colonies on 31 March 1957.

In 1946, the Loi Lamine Guèye granted some limited citizenship rights to natives of the African colonies. Later that year, each territory was for the first time able to elect local representatives to General Councils, though on a limited franchise. These bodies had only limited consultative powers, although they did approve local budgets.

Since Mali's independence there have been four rebellions involving Tuareg people, in 1962 to 1964, 1990 to 1995, 2007 to 2009, and since 2012. In the 2012 conflict in the north, cases of kidnapping and rape increased, and some ex-slaves were reportedly recaptured by their former masters. Islamist groups that had helped the rebels defeat the government turned on the Tuareg and took control of the north in order to impose sharia. Mali's economic and civil liberties gains, seen after the 1991 democratic transition, began to reverse after 2012.

Mauritania withdrew from the Economic Community of West African States (ECOWAS) in 1999. Because of its increasingly close ties to the Arab World, it is now often considered, especially in Africa, part of western North Africa.

After the 1960 revision of the French constitution, Senegal and former French Sudan became the Mali Federation, which lasted from 1960 to 1961. Ivory Coast, Niger, Upper Volta and Dahomey formed the short-lived Sahel-Benin Union, later the Conseil de l'Entente.

In August 1940, Free French General Charles de Gaulle suggested an overland campaign, landing at Conakry in French Guinea. He expected popular support for Free France to build during a drive on Dakar. British desires to move swiftly overruled his suggestion.
politics.source_title: French West Africa in World War II

philosophy.text: African philosophy's modern renaissance is linked to the 1920s, when Africans who had studied in the United States and Europe returned home. They had reflected on the racial discrimination they experienced abroad, and this stirred a feeling called onuma, meaning frustration. It inspired a systematic beginning of philosophizing African identity.

Akan philosophy, from the Akan people of West Africa, has been especially influential in modern discussions of personhood. Philosophers such as Kwasi Wiredu argue that personhood exists in degrees. In this view it is something a human becomes to different degrees through individual achievement.

Islam is the main religion of West Africa today, and in Africa it has often adapted to local cultural contexts and belief systems. This has formed Africa's own orthodoxies. A 2024 survey put Mali at 90% Muslim and Senegal at 89%.

Timbuktu's manuscripts, kept for centuries in private homes in northern Mali, include works on art, medicine, philosophy and science as well as copies of the Quran. Some are written in African languages such as Songhay and Bambara using Arabic script, known as Ajami. Their dates run to the early 20th century.

The term University of Sankore was popularised in 1961 by Ghanaian politician Kwame Nkrumah. Yet there is no evidence that an organised institution equivalent to a university ever existed in Timbuktu. The term persists as an expression of the scholarship achieved by the city's scholars and students.

During the Mali War, 4,203 of Timbuktu's manuscripts were burned or stolen between 2012 and 2013. Some 350,000 manuscripts were moved to safety, and 300,000 of them were still in Bamako in 2022. The rescue efforts by Haidara and others are told in Charlie English's 2017 book The Book Smugglers of Timbuktu.

culture.text: West Africa is home to many ethnic groups, including the Hausa, Yoruba, Igbo, Fulani, Akan, Mandé, Wolof, Songhai, Kanuri, Zarma and Tuareg. The most common religions in the region are Islam, Christianity and traditional African religions.

Although West Africa's cultures vary widely from Nigeria through to Senegal, they share general similarities in dress, cuisine, music and culture. These similarities are not shared extensively with groups outside the region, and the exchange behind them is a long one.
The board game oware takes its name from the Akan people of Ghana. Virtually all African peoples have some version of the game.
West Africa's major multi-sport event is the ECOWAS Games. It began with the 2012 ECOWAS Games.
A 2024 survey listed Mali at 90% and Senegal at 89% Muslim. Islam is the main religion of West Africa as of 2025.

In most African states Sharia is limited to personal-status law, covering marriage, divorce, inheritance and child custody. The article names northern Nigeria as the exception in West Africa, where secularism does not seem safe from the Islamic revival.

A joint project of Goethe University and Nigeria's National Commission for Museums and Monuments, running since 2005, found that more than 90% of known Nok sites in its research area had been illegally looted. Over 1,000 Nok terracotta sculptures have been smuggled abroad, and workshops also fake Nok sculptures and sell them as authentic.
tags: National Commission for Museums and Monuments

culture.text: French archaeologists began excavating Koumbi Saleh in the 1920s, and Paul Thomassey and Raymond Mauny dug there in 1949 and 1950. Controversy continues over whether it was the capital of the Ghana Empire, and the royal town's palace and burial mounds have not been located.

The influence of the Korings and Nyanchos of the old Mandinka federation of Kaabu is still embedded in the sociocultural fabric of post-independence Senegal, Gambia and Guinea-Bissau. The Nyancho were a warrior aristocracy made rich by slaves captured in war, and Kaabu's wars of expansion produced up to half of the African people sold into slavery during the 17th and 18th centuries. Its remaining kingdoms lasted until the British, Portuguese and French colonial powers arrived around the turn of the 20th century.

Nigeria repossessed five Nok statuettes in 2013, after a French thief looted them in August 2010. French customs agents had seized the pieces, and they were repatriated under a Nigerian Government Directive.
tags: Nigerian Federal Ministry of Information and National Orientation
